blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
blogs.description: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant…
blogs.content:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

 Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

 Coding agents in November 2025

 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

 In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

 Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

 This held up.

 Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

 Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

 The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

 Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

 The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

 Fable class models in June/July

 We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

 In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

 After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

 For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

 A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

 Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

 I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

 These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

 3D modeling and game development in September/October

 Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

 I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

 Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

 I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

 Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

 Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

 Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

 The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster .

 It feels like another inflection point to me.

 Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

 I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

 I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

 It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

 If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

 Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

blogs.description: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML…
blogs.content:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS .

 This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

 I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

 Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude):

 Ladybird (72925) [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926) [61 MB]
 ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB]
 ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB]
 ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB]
 ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB]
 ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB]
 ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB]
 ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB]
 ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB]
 ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB]
 ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB]
 ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB]
 ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB]
 ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB]
 └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB]
 Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

 I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

 The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

 undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

 I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.

 The October explosion

 The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

 Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

 That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

 This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!

 How did they do that? Coding agents:

 Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing .

 I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

 Should you use Ladybird?

 Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

 This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

 We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

 Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

 I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

blogs.content:
Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0

 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin.

 You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this:

 The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows.

 Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch.

 As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others.

 The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows.

 The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set.

 I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible.

blogs.content:
You Are the Irritant

 Last month, I gave a talk at the Cloud-Native Geospatial Forum titled, “Using AI Without Losing Your Humanity.” The big question I keep coming back to is how we work with AI, leverage it, and benefit from it without losing ourselves. It turns out we’ve faced this problem before. We have a long history of learning from weirdness and then paving over it, and we have a long history of building tools to get weird again.

 Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. You can also watch the talk on YouTube .

 As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions . I really appreciate it.

---

 Often, I wonder: how do we work with AI, benefit from it, without losing ourselves?

 My handwriting used to be pretty good. But as I entered high school and began typing more and more, my skill atrophied. Today, my handwriting is sloppy, only used for scratch notes or filling out forms.

 When I first got an iPhone, Google Maps felt like a superpower. The ability to instantly know where you are and be told where you need to go meant I didn’t have to memorize streets. I still learned geography, but not as well.

 When we cede a task to technology, our own ability atrophies. For handwriting, I’m more than okay with this trade. For navigation, slightly less so.

 With AI, this trade-off comes up quite a bit. Every now and then, I’ll hesitate to offload a task. Is this something I’m okay ceding? Is this something I’m okay forgetting how to do? Maybe it’s okay just this once .

 To be clear: I use AI heavily . I am not a hardcore skeptic. But still… The question of when to cede and when to grab the controls sometimes is easy, other times it’s anxiety inducing. Some days you wake up and think, “This is all going to be great. It’s just normal technology.” And the next day you wake up and, well. There are better days.

 Thankfully there is plenty of precendent. We, as humans, have navigated similar situations many times before.

---

 Yesterday I ran an experiment to understand the reliability and ‘averaging’ nature of AI systems.

 I gave a coding agent a simple prompt: “Make me a website landing page for a B2B CRM company.” This is what I got. It looks pretty good! Out of the box, that’s pretty amazing.

---

 Then I completely cleared the cache, stood up another session (with absolutely no record of the first), and gave it the exact same prompt.

 I got almost exactly the same thing. The headline was a little different.

---

 What’s funny is that as I kept doing this, the idea of “the CRM your team will actually use” kept coming up over and over again. The font was always the same. The highlight color was always the same. The same statistical and customer proof points showed up every time. The model reasons its way through all of this, crunches it all, and produces… Squarespace templates with extra steps.

 (The dark themed versions appeared during a later session that took place around 11pm. I later confirmed the model was noting the system time when running commands like ls , and that was enough to nudge it into dark mode.)

---

 On one hand, we love the consistency of AI (it follows instructions reliably), but on the other hand it gives us similar slop if we aren’t careful.

 Consider the “AI Poster.” You can go to Shanghai, San Francisco, New York, or Australia and you’ll see these same posters everywhere. The people creating them write weak, small prompts and don’t iterate. What they get back is the default. The default aesthetic smell.

 And it seems like we’re getting more and more of this. Early image models were weird . We got more fingers, but we also got unruly output. Which at least felt novel. Today, we get the same websites, the same slides, and the same posters .

---

 So why is this happening?

 It’s happening because the labs are trading diversity for reliability.

---

 And honestly, it makes sense. In the early days of ChatGPT, it was really hard to generate polished images or good code. You had to write long, detailed prompts. Prompting was a skill. And this makes your market smaller.

 The labs need to build products that work for a layperson who types, “Make me a website, don’t make mistakes.” And they also need to work for seasoned developers, who give longer, thoughtful, context-rich instructions.

 All the labs are doing this. They’re turning their models from infrastructure into appliances. The goal is to produce the most reliable, most consistently approved output.

---

 We’ve done this before. In fact, we do it all the time. The history of the world is full of weird deviations that generate lots of interesting ideas. We take the best ones, formalize them, and scale them up.

 This is Frederick Taylor .

 Taylor is one of the fathers of time and motion studies, processes for analyzing informal work behavior and standardizing it into one optimal routine. He was obsessed with efficiency and would show up at factories with a stopwatch. He hated the idea that craftspeople came up with one-off solutions, their own ways of working. He wanted to analyze these unique habits and boil them down to a perfect method that could be repeated over and over again.

---

 Interestingly, for a man searching for the one perfect method, Taylor had a competitor doing very similar work at the exact same time. Frank Gilbreth made prettier pictures.

 Taylor had his stopwatch. Gilbreth had his chronocyclographs . He attached lights to workers’ heads and hands, went to bricklayers, and said, “Go lay some bricks.” He watched what happened, over and over again, and got bricklaying down from 18 motions to an optimal handful.

---

 This became the field of time and motion studies. You got these MTM tables , which still exist today.

---

 Then we got factories built on these ideas. Taylor’s goal was to remove inefficient work and one-off solutions to find the one best way.

---

 Like the labs today, factories formalized everything and traded diversity for efficiency.

 And it worked! No one’s going to argue against the scale of output from the industrial revolution. But there were downsides. We formalized all the weirdness, and the weirdness was what drove innovation. We took away the things that gave us the good ideas, the ones that defined the process that turned out to be the “best.”

 Once that’s gone, where do the new ideas come from? We have to wait longer. We have to work harder. When you decouple the doing from the thinking, you get into trouble.

---

 Let’s go back to geospatial for a second. This is a desire path . Desire paths are the unofficial routes we want to take. They don’t appear until enough people keep walking them.

 If you’re a city planner or architect, what do you do when a desire path shows up and ruins your garden? You can be antagonistic and put up fences to enforce the “official” path.

 Or you can pave it. You say, “All right, that’s where people want to walk. We’ll pave it.” And that ends up being a pretty good idea.

---

 These are called sneckdowns . Traffic calming and safety planners look at how fresh snow gets worn down to see where cars drive, where they don’t drive, and where people walk. Then they use those cues to design traffic calming measures.

 This is a great example of formalization. We’re taking away the weirdness, but we’re meeting the weirdness where it is.

---

 An architecture firm in Helsinki did this when they completely redesigned a train station plaza. Unfortunately, they took the after shot from a different angle, so it’s hard to see how the two map onto each other. But it’s a nice story.

---

 The problem is that once we pave these paths, they stop being information layers. The signal came from the deviation. The signal came from the desire path. Once the desire path is paved, even with all the benefits this brings, we don’t know where the next signal will come from.

---

 When we feel constrained, we seek deviation. Humans have dealt with this forever. We even make tools for deviation.

 If I want to find a new desire path and everything’s already paved over, what do I do?

---

 Perhaps we might turn to one of our oldest tools for deviation, as old as civilization itself: alcohol. As Homer Simpson once said: the cause of, and solution to, all of life’s problems.

 Alcohol is a classic tool for deviation. Sober people take the paved route. If you get drunk, you might start wandering in weird directions. There’s a term for this: the drunkard’s walk.

 History is full of examples. Ancient historians claimed the Persians would get drunk the night before a battle to come up with crazy plans. The next day they’d review them sober: “All right, five of these sucked, but this one’s really good.”

---

 In the 1950s, Guy Debord looked at all the urban planning and maps of Paris and found them so staid and sterile. So he decided to make his own map by deliberately wandering in the weirdest patterns possible. These mostly ended up being bar crawls, but that’s okay. He encoded them in an abstract, performance-art map he called The Naked City .

---

 It’s a sort of radical act of reinterpreting the city. Debord found his own desire paths, with alcohol as the instigator.

 Innovation through irritation.

---

 Let’s go back to AI.

 AI is a giant formalization machine. It finds the one good way. The labs try to work around this by saying, “If you put in a lot of instructions, it’ll follow them.” But if you don’t, and most people don’t, you get the default.

---

 How many of you have seen the meme on the left? It’s one of my favorites. It comes from an old image model that took pixelated photos and tried to upscale them, filling in the average. We wanted Obama. But the model chose the average, the in-distribution option, this dude on the right.

 Earlier this year, at a conference on compound AI systems , one of the lead developers of Claude Code put up the slide on the right. It’s my favorite slide I’ve seen from Anthropic, because it puts a finger on exactly the problem we’ve been discussing: “Every gap you leave, Claude fills with an in-distribution choice.”

 In machine learning, “in-distribution” means the things the model knows : the average, what it’s learned. If you don’t define something, it’s going to give you the in-distribution choice.

 Since that slide went up, Anthropic has been nudging people in the opposite direction . Boris Cherny told a YC audience to delete their CLAUDE.md , skills, and hooks every six months and “see what the model does.” The Claude Code team wrote that they’d been “overconstraining” Claude and cut over 80% of their own system prompt. For most people, most of the time, this might be more reliable.

 But I beg you not to do this when it matters.

---

 Because what you get is this: the same posters, everywhere. And these posters could be your software. They could be your emails, the letters you write to people, or the plans you come up with.

 That’s bad. And that’s just the local level, where your work starts to suck.

 On the global level, it’s every town having the same posters. That’s what’s happening on the internet right now. People write newsletters with bots so other bots can read them. Then the models all train on each other, and we get the same things over and over again.

---

 Here’s a quote I saw last week and absolutely love. There’s a site called delve.town where bots built on different models talk to each other. And recently, many of the open models have started writing in the same broken, symbolic, overwrought language Opus 5 uses.

 Julia, a researcher at Anthropic, comments: “An unfortunate consequence of rampant distillation from Claude is that when we screwed up its ability to speak like a normal person earlier this year the entire ecosystem went down with us.”

 It’s very true. We see this over and over again.

---

 Left unchecked, AI overwhelms us with the average, both locally and globally. We need to fix that.

---

 JENSEN HUANG & NVIDIA

 Since Thursday:

 I have created a Sharp Studio service application that manages all of the Sharp Tech studio cameras, lights, mixer, and various other devices. That service can be accessed by a Windows app on the studio PC, an iPhone app, a web app, or an Elgato Stream Deck; every device in the room needed to record an episode is fully remote controlled.

 I have created multiple single-use iOS apps for cataloguing and measuring items and designed and 3D-printed a measurement rig. I have also designed and purchased the items for several dedicated hardware devices, including a device for direct interaction with an agent, and dedicated display devices for the studio.

 I have created a full-fledged iOS app (designed for the Duo, but it works on regular iPhones) for accessing the various computers I manage; it works across screen sharing, terminals, and KVM switches. It works on Mac, Linux, and Windows. I honestly think it’s the best screen sharing client ever made. I already use it daily.

 Along the way I created a small harness for my agent such that it not only choreographs subagents, but also farms out work to various computers I own, depending on the load: a Mac for iOS development, a gaming PC for GPU-related work, and a Linux server for everything else. That work is tracked on a custom status board that runs on every TV in my house, as an iOS app, and as a Telegram bot.

 All of this would have taken teams of people weeks of work, if not months, just a few years ago; I, however, have AI. It only takes an individual.

 The Deflationary Employee

 The largest company of the 1950s, as measured by market capitalization, was AT&T; in 1959 it had revenue of $7.54 billion and a market cap of $17.1 billion. It had 729,000 employees. In inflation-adjusted terms that’s revenue of $87.5 billion and a market cap of $198.4 billion; we don’t apply inflation to employees.

 Or, maybe we do, but in the other direction: what has been striking about the most valuable companies in the world is how their employee numbers have deflated , even as their revenue and market cap have exploded. All dollar numbers in this table are inflation-adjusted to today:

 This translates into a stunning rise in revenue/employee and market cap/employee — note that this graph is a logarithmic scale:

 And yet, even this chart, which pegs the market cap/employee of Nvidia at $95 million, doesn’t come close to what the market decided one particular Nvidia employee is worth:

 As ChatGPT, which helped me make these charts, helpfully noted:

 Nvidia gained nearly $1 trillion in market capitalization following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. That gain alone exceeds the entire inflation-adjusted market capitalization of ExxonMobil in 2008 ($638 billion).

 It only takes an individual.

 The Huang Odyssey

 To describe the two-week odyssey of Nvidia’s then-and-now-CEO Jensen Huang as surreal is an understatement; what you can’t argue, however, is that it was unprecedented: it was only three Thanksgivings ago that Sam Altman was deposed and reinstated as OpenAI CEO over the very same weekend (two Max Verstappen Las Vegas Grand Prix wins, I might note).

 That said, I didn’t think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech : whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company’s investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act. And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I’ve invoked the phrase “Show me the man and I’ll show you the crime” over the past few weeks, but it’s worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, “Which one?”, at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned.

 At the same time, it sure seemed like no one cared about Huang’s affairs, including those with subordinates; the real crime appeared to be Huang’s resolute advocacy for selling chips to China, his refusal to do any more than the bare minimum to abide by export control rules, and, his most ardent critics allege, turning a blind eye towards actual smuggling.

 I’m not here, today at least, to litigate these accusations; I covered much of it in last week’s Article Obituaries (alternate title for today: Resurrections ). And, more broadly, this isn’t an Article focused on normative analysis; Huang’s Chinese interactions are going to be investigated by a Democratic Congress empowered by the anti-AI wave at the ballot box, and his personal moral failings would, for nearly any other executive, leave no question about the inevitability of their early retirement.

 Rather, I am struck by the extent to which Huang is, quite obviously, not any other executive, and how his reinstatement is the apotheosis of how tech is transforming business, just as AI is the apotheosis of information technology. It only takes an individual.

 The End of Managerialism

 In 1941, James Burnham, a former Trotskyist, wrote The Managerial Revolution , where he argued that the increasing complexity of industrial society, what with its massive returns to scale, technological complexity, and enmeshment with government, would increasingly divide owners of the means of production from the managerial class that actually controlled society. In this view Soviet communism, German fascism, and American New Dealism were all heads of the same hydra, different ideologies justifying the same inevitable structural transformation of society from individualism and entrepreneurship to corporatism and bureaucracy.

 Over the ensuing 85 years, it’s hard to argue that Burnham didn’t have a point, and for the last 10 days, it appeared as if the managerial state — the blob, to use Washington D.C.’s terms, or the deep state, to use its opponents’ — had slain arguably the single greatest challenge to Burnham’s thesis. Huang was explicit about the fact that Nvidia was designed as a vehicle for a singular individual — Huang — to enact his vision for the future of computing. This is a long excerpt, but I think an important one, from the Stratechery Interview with Tae Kim about his book The Nvidia Way :

 So if this analogy is correct, the Apple one, does this make you more optimistic or less optimistic about Nvidia in a post-Jensen world, whenever that arrives? Another analogy that Jensen’s talked about, “It’s we, not I”, and that’s a very Apple-like thing too, famously not saying who did what. But the net result is that just meant Steve Jobs got credited for everything and there’s a bit now, “Well, Jensen Huang gets credited for everything”, but then you’re almost making the case, “Well actually, that’s probably deserved”. Then again, Apple, at least financially, has done very well in this post-Steve Jobs era, and yet when you are listing companies that Nvidia employees go to when they feel like they don’t fit in, you said Apple, and maybe they would’ve felt differently fifteen years ago. What’s your view going forward?

 TK: Financially, I agree with you, but if you take a step back, what has Apple created in terms of innovation? They’re just so far behind in everything and they’re running on this platform that Steve Jobs laid the foundation and created, there isn’t really anything new. The Apple Car kind of fell apart, they’re nowhere in AI. So, yes, the Apple iPhone is this amazing platform that Tim Cook’s been able to shepherd and make hundreds of billions of dollars, etc., but in terms of actual technology innovations, I think it’s hard-pressed to say that Apple has really innovated.

 But in a similar vein with Nvidia, if say Jensen disappears tomorrow and decides to retire, which is not going to happen because he loves Nvidia, but say that he does, I don’t know, Jensen is so ingrained. Part of why Nvidia is so able to do what it does is that he is so ingrained and has his finger on the pulse of everything that happens in the company…

 He’s fashioned Nvidia. Nvidia, it’s like an exoskeleton for him.

 TK: That exact analogy, he says he built Nvidia, where he’s like the race car driver of a Formula One car. He literally says that, like, “I built Nvidia in a way where I could drive it, and manage it, and steer it perfectly”. So, without Jensen there, do I see another CEO that’s reading 100 top-five emails a day, that is looking at all the AI discussion email lists inside a company, trading AI papers with his top engineers? I don’t know. I’ve met all the top Nvidia people, they’re all impressive, but they’re not on the Jensen level.

 It goes back to the functional organization bit. You get a bunch of people who are absolute best in their field and so you, as the person in the center that is involved in everything, has awareness of everything, gets to direct the best possible resource at every sort of opportunity. But that, by definition, means there isn’t space in the organization for other generalists, right?

 This was a thing at Apple, again just to go back to that analogy. And again, this was fifteen years ago, when Steve Jobs was still there so probably a bit of a different world. But there was a very sort of stern, “This is not the place for generalists”, like, “You come here to be a specialist, if you get a job here, you should expect you’ll never have a different job because we want you to be the best at what you do, we’re not interested in multiple experiences across business units and things along those lines”. But that works when it’s all flowing up to one node that is the ultimate generalist that has the view and understanding of everything and it’s incredibly effective. But yeah, it’s not good for succession planning, it makes it pretty tough.

 And yet, despite Nvidia’s reliance on Huang, the board and the powers that be decided he had to go, in direct opposition to the preferences of Nvidia’s nominal owners, i.e. shareholders. And, like I said, I thought they had succeeded; tech may have made it increasingly possible for a dwindling number of employees to deliver outsized revenue and valuations, but ultimately any individual would be deemed expendable, particularly in the face of a coordinated media campaign and the opposition of the national security apparatus.

 But I was wrong. And, ultimately, even if you think what happened this weekend was wrong — including President Trump calling into an Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s reinstatement — this moment does strike me as both unique in terms of the clear exception that Huang has obviously been deemed to be (and not without merit), and also a harbinger of the future. It only takes an individual.

 The Bimodal Distribution

 The world is, make no mistake, growing more complex. The tools we have to master that complexity, however, are not just improving, they actually thrive on complexity. When I’m trying to teach someone how to use AI, one of my first pieces of advice is to talk more (and yes, talking is better than typing); you can’t overwhelm the AI with information, it’s dealing in information at an unimaginable scale. Whatever pittance...

This translates into a stunning rise in revenue/employee and market cap/employee — note that this graph is a logarithmic scale:

And yet, even this chart, which pegs the market cap/employee of Nvidia at $95 million, doesn’t come close to what the market decided one particular Nvidia employee is worth:

As ChatGPT, which helped me make these charts, helpfully noted:

Nvidia gained nearly $1 trillion in market capitalization following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO. That gain alone exceeds the entire inflation-adjusted market capitalization of ExxonMobil in 2008 ($638 billion).

It only takes an individual.

The Huang Odyssey

To describe the two-week odyssey of Nvidia’s then-and-now-CEO Jensen Huang as surreal is an understatement; what you can’t argue, however, is that it was unprecedented: it was only three Thanksgivings ago that Sam Altman was deposed and reinstated as OpenAI CEO over the very same weekend (two Max Verstappen Las Vegas Grand Prix wins, I might note).

That said, I didn’t think that this episode would end the same way, and said as much on Sharp Tech : whereas Altman was taken out by a somewhat ham-fisted internal coup and restored through pressure from the private company’s investors and employees, Huang appeared to be targeted by a much more systemic campaign by powerful actors leveraging the media and barely disguised insinuations of malfeasance to leave the Nvidia board with no choice but to act. And, to be sure, Huang gave his enemies plenty of ammunition; I’ve invoked the phrase “Show me the man and I’ll show you the crime” over the past few weeks, but it’s worth acknowledging that Huang basically asked his critics, “Which one?”, at least as far as his sexual proclivities were concerned.

At the same time, it sure seemed like no one cared about Huang’s affairs, including those with subordinates; the real crime appeared to be Huang’s resolute advocacy for selling chips to China, his refusal to do any more than the bare minimum to abide by export control rules, and, his most ardent critics allege, turning a blind eye towards actual smuggling.

I’m not here, today at least, to litigate these accusations; I covered much of it in last week’s Article Obituaries (alternate title for today: Resurrections ). And, more broadly, this isn’t an Article focused on normative analysis; Huang’s Chinese interactions are going to be investigated by a Democratic Congress empowered by the anti-AI wave at the ballot box, and his personal moral failings would, for nearly any other executive, leave no question about the inevitability of their early retirement.

Rather, I am struck by the extent to which Huang is, quite obviously, not any other executive, and how his reinstatement is the apotheosis of how tech is transforming business, just as AI is the apotheosis of information technology. It only takes an individual.

The End of Managerialism

In 1941, James Burnham, a former Trotskyist, wrote The Managerial Revolution , where he argued that the increasing complexity of industrial society, what with its massive returns to scale, technological complexity, and enmeshment with government, would increasingly divide owners of the means of production from the managerial class that actually controlled society. In this view Soviet communism, German fascism, and American New Dealism were all heads of the same hydra, different ideologies justifying the same inevitable structural transformation of society from individualism and entrepreneurship to corporatism and bureaucracy.

Over the ensuing 85 years, it’s hard to argue that Burnham didn’t have a point, and for the last 10 days, it appeared as if the managerial state — the blob, to use Washington D.C.’s terms, or the deep state, to use its opponents’ — had slain arguably the single greatest challenge to Burnham’s thesis. Huang was explicit about the fact that Nvidia was designed as a vehicle for a singular individual — Huang — to enact his vision for the future of computing. This is a long excerpt, but I think an important one, from the Stratechery Interview with Tae Kim about his book The Nvidia Way :

So if this analogy is correct, the Apple one, does this make you more optimistic or less optimistic about Nvidia in a post-Jensen world, whenever that arrives? Another analogy that Jensen’s talked about, “It’s we, not I”, and that’s a very Apple-like thing too, famously not saying who did what. But the net result is that just meant Steve Jobs got credited for everything and there’s a bit now, “Well, Jensen Huang gets credited for everything”, but then you’re almost making the case, “Well actually, that’s probably deserved”. Then again, Apple, at least financially, has done very well in this post-Steve Jobs era, and yet when you are listing companies that Nvidia employees go to when they feel like they don’t fit in, you said Apple, and maybe they would’ve felt differently fifteen years ago. What’s your view going forward?

TK: Financially, I agree with you, but if you take a step back, what has Apple created in terms of innovation? They’re just so far behind in everything and they’re running on this platform that Steve Jobs laid the foundation and created, there isn’t really anything new. The Apple Car kind of fell apart, they’re nowhere in AI. So, yes, the Apple iPhone is this amazing platform that Tim Cook’s been able to shepherd and make hundreds of billions of dollars, etc., but in terms of actual technology innovations, I think it’s hard-pressed to say that Apple has really innovated.

But in a similar vein with Nvidia, if say Jensen disappears tomorrow and decides to retire, which is not going to happen because he loves Nvidia, but say that he does, I don’t know, Jensen is so ingrained. Part of why Nvidia is so able to do what it does is that he is so ingrained and has his finger on the pulse of everything that happens in the company…

He’s fashioned Nvidia. Nvidia, it’s like an exoskeleton for him.

TK: That exact analogy, he says he built Nvidia, where he’s like the race car driver of a Formula One car. He literally says that, like, “I built Nvidia in a way where I could drive it, and manage it, and steer it perfectly”. So, without Jensen there, do I see another CEO that’s reading 100 top-five emails a day, that is looking at all the AI discussion email lists inside a company, trading AI papers with his top engineers? I don’t know. I’ve met all the top Nvidia people, they’re all impressive, but they’re not on the Jensen level.

It goes back to the functional organization bit. You get a bunch of people who are absolute best in their field and so you, as the person in the center that is involved in everything, has awareness of everything, gets to direct the best possible resource at every sort of opportunity. But that, by definition, means there isn’t space in the organization for other generalists, right?

This was a thing at Apple, again just to go back to that analogy. And again, this was fifteen years ago, when Steve Jobs was still there so probably a bit of a different world. But there was a very sort of stern, “This is not the place for generalists”, like, “You come here to be a specialist, if you get a job here, you should expect you’ll never have a different job because we want you to be the best at what you do, we’re not interested in multiple experiences across business units and things along those lines”. But that works when it’s all flowing up to one node that is the ultimate generalist that has the view and understanding of everything and it’s incredibly effective. But yeah, it’s not good for succession planning, it makes it pretty tough.

And yet, despite Nvidia’s reliance on Huang, the board and the powers that be decided he had to go, in direct opposition to the preferences of Nvidia’s nominal owners, i.e. shareholders. And, like I said, I thought they had succeeded; tech may have made it increasingly possible for a dwindling number of employees to deliver outsized revenue and valuations, but ultimately any individual would be deemed expendable, particularly in the face of a coordinated media campaign and the opposition of the national security apparatus.

But I was wrong. And, ultimately, even if you think what happened this weekend was wrong — including President Trump calling into an Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s reinstatement — this moment does strike me as both unique in terms of the clear exception that Huang has obviously been deemed to be (and not without merit), and also a harbinger of the future. It only takes an individual.

The Bimodal Distribution

The world is, make no mistake, growing more complex. The tools we have to master that complexity, however, are not just improving, they actually thrive on complexity. When I’m trying to teach someone how to use AI, one of my first pieces of advice is to talk more (and yes, talking is better than typing); you can’t overwhelm the AI with information, it’s dealing in information at an unimaginable scale....

Amazon makes the case they are not like other compute providers, even as they signal the willingness to give up margin to serve the frontier.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I continue to discuss the Jensen Huang situation, why I think everyone is thinking about agentic commerce wrong, and why I love the iPhone Duo.

Then, on Sunday’s subscriber only mailbag , we discuss our decision to embrace video, whether disruption theory is still real, and the challenge of selling AI using worse AI.

This week is the Thanksgiving holiday; there will be an Update today and tomorrow only, and no Stratechery Interview. There will also be one Dithering episode on Tuesday, and a subscriber-only Sharp Tech on Wednesday.

On to the Update:

Amazon Earnings

It was, needless to say, a very busy November; so busy, in fact, that I am only just now getting to Amazon’s earnings, which dropped at the end of October. From Bloomberg :

Amazon.com Inc. shares dropped after the company reported greater capital spending than anticipated and the slowest growth in the core e-commerce business in three years. Amazon said it spent more than $77 billion on property and equipment in the third quarter, far more than analysts’ estimates, while pursuing its effort to build data centers and fulfill demand for artificial intelligence services. Third-quarter sales were lower than anticipated, rising 12% to $201.9 billion.

Revenue at the cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, accelerated for the sixth straight quarter. Online sales gained just 2% to $68.5 billion, the lowest increase since early 2023, when Amazon was still working through the post-pandemic slump in online retail. Advertising sales, a business closely tied to the e-commerce franchise, rose 11%, the slowest rate since Amazon began breaking out such results in 2020. The shares fell 4.4% to $233.10 as the markets opened in New York on Friday. The stock is up about 1% so far this year.

CEO Andy Jassy did not reassure investors on the earnings call about Amazon’s spending; in fact, he doubled down:

On the CapEx involved to grow the way we’re talking about, it’s meaningful. And I think that this — the way we think about it, Doug, is that this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. I think what we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime. And if the idea of being able to grow 39% with $184 billion annual run rate and to grow 40% a year on top of that in each of the next 2 years and ultimately end up as $1 trillion-plus business, we’re going to invest to continue being the leader.

We are the leader today in the, I’ll call it, the infrastructure and AI space. And would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yes, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity. And we can fund this plan. And I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue. It will forever change our free cash flow. And we’re going to invest and we’re going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.

The part that I thought was notable — and very much in line with a lot of the analysis I’ve been doing on Stratechery this year — was Jassy’s implicit assumption that AI compute is on its way to being a commodity business; this was in response to a question about workloads running on Bedrock, AWS’s managed inference service:

Well, you’re right that the majority and most of Bedrock today is being run on top of Trainium. And we do that in meaningful part because we really like the price performance that we’re getting, and it allows us to both keep prices as low as possible for customers as well as we like the margins associated with it.

If you think about margins in the cloud space and you’re looking at different players and what their cost structure looks like, there are a few things to pay attention to. The first is for their data centers, how many of them are they actually buying or long leasing versus doing colo or neoclouds. I mean neoclouds are about 3,500 basis points worse in operating margin than if you long lease them. And then you look at what is the hardware on top of which they’re running, and if you’re using the hardware that everybody else is using, you’ll have a comparable cost structure to what everybody is doing. And if you have the ability to use hardware that’s different, you’ll have an advantage.

And so I think when you look at what we’re doing, most of our capacity is either owned or long leased which enjoys better operating margins than what you’ll find when people are mostly doing colo or neo or a big chunk doing colo or neo. And the fact that we’re running on top of our own chip that’s providing both advantaged price performance and it’s more cost effective for ourselves because we own it, I think, gives us some structural cost advantages that I think are going to be very helpful to customers as we pass them back to customers and helpful to the overall economics of AWS.

This is the bull case not for a time when compute is scarce, but for when compute is abundant, which, incidentally, is exactly what investors are freaking out about right now. In a commodity market price is not based on differentiation but rather marginal willingness to pay: how much is the last entity willing to pay for a unit of compute? And, if we were to enter a scenario where there simply aren’t enough entities for all of the compute that is available, then the price will fall to the marginal cost of the compute that clears the market; everyone whose marginal cost exceeds that will simply not sell. Everyone who can’t make enough operating profit to pay for their debt load will go bankrupt.

However, that doesn’t mean there won’t be real money to be made in such a market; profit will be a function of having a superior cost structure, which is exactly what Jassy is claiming AWS will have. Moreover, the entities with the superior cost structures will be the last to lose demand, precisely because they will have the most capacity to handle lower prices (indeed, they will attract it, because they will be safe to build on).

Meanwhile, Jassy continued to make the case — reasonably, I think — that inference benefits AWS broadly:

We have a compelling flywheel spinning in AWS. Borrowing from Jim Collins’ flywheel definition Good to Great, where if you do A, you almost can’t help but do B and if you do B, you almost can’t help but do C and so on. In AWS, having the leading functionality, security and operational performance can’t help but drive customers to run their apps and store their data in AWS, which can’t help but drive AWS AI demand because customers prefer their production inference to be near the rest of their data and apps, which can’t help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, posttraining and tool usage, which can’t help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality.

This is a different model than primarily hosting GPUs or renting short-term data center capacity. This is a long-term platform strategy that broadly helps customers invent and evolve their customer experiences, operate stably and build a reliable partnership they can grow for many years. And it also yields very attractive long-term economics for us regardless of supply scarcity.

Or, per the point above, regardless of supply abundance! In short, Jassy’s overarching point seemed to be, “We are not the neoclouds”, and he’s right!

The Chip Question

Jassy confirmed that Amazon will be selling Trainium chips:

Customers using our custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in Q3 alone, and we just open-sourced TorchNeuron so developers can run existing PyTorch code, which most already use on Trainium without rewriting a thing. As we launch new generations of chips, demand for prior generations remained strong. After our launch of Graviton5, backlog for prior generation Graviton instances still more than doubled quarter-over-quarter. And short-term capacity for prior generation Trainium instances sell at a premium compared to the first half of the year. With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027. Overall demand for AWS capacity remains exceptionally strong.

An analyst reasonably asked why, if inference demand is so strong, AWS wouldn’t just keep Trainium for itself; Jassy’s answer wasn’t very convincing:

On the balance of chips and what you sell externally versus what you use inside your cloud, it’s a very good question. And it’s a question that we’re continuing to evaluate as we speak. I would say that the number of companies who have a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two. So there really aren’t many customers that have to grapple with the same type of problem at this type of scale.

And at this point, everybody is producing their advanced chips with the same provider. There’s only so many chips that provider can provide each year. Everybody gets an allocation. And you have to decide with that allocation how much of it you want to sell externally and how much of it you want to use in your cloud. And there’s a trade-off. If you sell externally, you’re able to realize more revenue in the short term because you get to recognize the revenue as soon as it leaves your inventory. And on the flip side, if you decide to use it inside your cloud in the form of EC2 instances or Bedrock, you actually will end up driving more absolute revenue and free cash flow from those chips because you get to use them over 5 to 6 years and drive revenue for a longer period of time. So you have to really think through what you want to do.

To date, I would say that we’ve taken a different approach in how we’ve used our chips than the other provider who has the same type of balancing act going on. And as I mentioned earlier, we believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally, and we’re going to start in late 2027. And we will be thinking through that balance, I think, probably every year. But they’ll both be very significant. Our ability to create price performance, scalable chips is going to be a very significant strategic advantage for us at scale, both in our own cost structure as well as building a separate business and selling external chips and selling external chips really is a very different business than your cloud infrastructure business.

I admit, posting that entire answer was kind of a waste of time, but it’s always funny when executives clearly don’t want to answer a specific question. And some of the points were accurate! Only Amazon and Google make their own LLM accelerators at scale, and both are dependent on TSMC in the end, and have to make hard allocation decisions. And, critically, both have to make the same allocation decision, which, I strongly suspect, is “Do we want to keep Anthropic as a customer?”.
